scope: 18 original taught first-school-mock Chemistry short flashcards from five AQA topic groupings: Ka/Kw and acid strength, chirality, carbonyl reduction and reactivity, carboxylic acid/ester functional recall, triglycerides and soaps. Improve actual production-marking examples without modifying original cards.
method: Check original ID, front, back, Chemistry subject, AS/A2 stage, active and mock eligibility before adding one correct rephrasing and two incorrect concepts to each existing card. Preserve prior accepted/rejected examples; verify all 54 responses using the real card evaluator.
limits: A targeted short-recall audit, not the complete AQA specification crosswalk.
No long-answer mechanism disguised as a flashcard.
Does not test every possible free-text wording, drawings or unseen calculations.
No edits to exam bank, original flashcard data, saved progress, XP or cloud sync.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.sourceTopic: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
accept: The dissociation equilibrium constant for an acid in aqueous solution.
reject: Ka is the ionic product of water rather than an acid dissociation constant.
Ka measures the equilibrium constant for a base accepting a proton.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does a larger Ka usually indicate?
rows.sourceTopic: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
accept: A higher Ka indicates a greater extent of weak-acid dissociation and therefore greater acid strength.
reject: A greater Ka means that a weak acid dissociates less and is weaker.
Ka has no relationship to the strength of an acid.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.sourceTopic: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
accept: At 298 K, Kw is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶.
reject: At 25 °C Kw equals 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol² dm⁻⁶.
Kw at 25 °C is the pH of pure water, so it equals 7.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is required for a common chiral carbon centre?
accept: A tetrahedral carbon atom bearing four different substituent groups can be chiral.
reject: Four identical groups around a carbon atom make it chiral.
A carbon with just two identical substituents is always chiral.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does a racemic mixture give no net optical rotation?
accept: Equal proportions of the two enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally and oppositely, giving no overall rotation.
reject: The two enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light in the same direction.
A racemic mixture rotates plane-polarised light twice as much as one pure enantiomer.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: Usually a carbon bonded to four different groups.
accept: A chiral carbon centre is typically bonded to four different groups.
reject: A carbon attached to four identical substituents is a chiral centre.
Any carbon–carbon double bond must contain a chiral centre.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why are carbonyl compounds attacked at carbon?
rows.originalBack: Their C=O bond is polar, with carbon δ+.
accept: The C=O bond is polar and the carbonyl carbon is partially positive, so nucleophiles attack that carbon.
reject: The carbonyl oxygen is partially positive, so nucleophiles attack oxygen instead of carbon.
A carbonyl double bond is non-polar and its carbon is electron-rich.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the functional group in an aldehyde?
accept: An aldehyde has a terminal carbonyl group written –CHO.
reject: An aldehyde must have a carbonyl carbon bonded to two other carbon atoms.
The aldehyde functional group is –COOH, including an –OH bond.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What forms when a ketone is reduced?
accept: Reduction of a ketone produces a secondary alcohol.
reject: Reduction of a ketone always makes a primary alcohol.
Reduction of a ketone forms a carboxylic acid.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What forms when an aldehyde is reduced?
accept: An aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol.
reject: An aldehyde is reduced to a secondary alcohol.
Reduction of an aldehyde directly produces an ester.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why do carboxylic acids react with carbonates?
rows.originalBack: Their acidic protons react with carbonate ions, releasing carbon dioxide.
accept: The acidic hydrogen reacts with carbonate ions and carbon dioxide gas is released.
reject: Carboxylic acids and carbonates react to release hydrogen gas but no carbon dioxide.
A carbonate is reduced to carbon metal when a weak carboxylic acid is added.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What numbering rule applies when naming a carboxylic acid?
rows.originalBack: The carbon in –COOH is carbon number 1.
accept: The carbon of the –COOH group is always carbon number one in a carboxylic acid chain.
reject: Number the carboxyl group carbon last, at the far end of the longest chain.
The –COOH carbon is not included when numbering the parent chain.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the ester functional group?
accept: An ester has a –C(=O)–O– linkage, commonly written R–COO–R′.
reject: An ester is identified by the –COOH group of a carboxylic acid.
The ester functional group is R–CO–R with no oxygen linkage between the groups.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Which acid-derived groups are joined to glycerol in a triglyceride?
accept: A triglyceride contains three long-chain fatty-acid residues ester-linked to glycerol.
reject: Three glycerol molecules are attached to one fatty-acid residue.
A triglyceride carries three phosphate groups instead of fatty-acid residues.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Can a triglyceride contain three different fatty acids?
rows.originalBack: Yes. The three long chains need not be identical.
accept: Yes, the three fatty-acid chains in a triglyceride can all be different.
reject: No, all three triglyceride fatty-acid chains must have identical structures.
No, a triglyceride can only contain one fatty-acid residue.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalBack: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats or oils.
accept: Saponification is alkaline hydrolysis of triglycerides or fats and oils.
reject: Saponification is the acid-catalysed formation of triglycerides from glycerol.
Saponification means breaking hydrocarbons into alkenes by cracking.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What are the main products of triglyceride saponification?
accept: The main products are glycerol and long-chain carboxylate salts, which are soaps.
reject: The only products of triglyceride saponification are glycerol and alkanes.
Saponification produces new triglycerides and water instead of soap.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does soap clean oily substances?
rows.originalBack: Its non-polar tail interacts with oil and its ionic head with water.
accept: The non-polar tail associates with oil while the ionic, hydrophilic head interacts with water.
reject: The ionic head dissolves in oil while the non-polar tail is attracted to water.
Soap contains no water-attracting part so it cannot help remove grease.
